_about: For each speaker in John: the language the words were most probably first spoken in, with a confidence label and the basis. The Gospel itself was composed and read in Greek (project finding 12), so the rendered voice is the Greek a first-century audience heard. This layer says what stood behind it.

default.basis: Aramaic was the everyday language of Jewish Palestine (Fitzmyer, 'The Languages of Palestine in the First Century AD'; Aramaic documents from Qumran, Murabba'at and Nahal Hever; ossuary inscriptions).

narrator.basis: The Gospel is a Greek composition: its word-chains exist only in Greek (finding 12) and all early manuscripts are Greek.

Jesus.basis: Aramaic sayings preserved in the Gospels (talitha koum, ephphatha, abba, eloi eloi lema sabachthani); the Aramaic words John keeps (rabbi, Messias, Kephas, rabbouni). Hebrew likely for scripture; Greek possible with Pilate and with 'the Greeks' (12:20).

John (the Baptist).basis: A Judean preacher to Judean crowds; his self-description quotes Isaiah 40:3, known in Hebrew and in the Aramaic targum tradition. Josephus (Antiquities 18.116-119) describes his preaching to the Jews.

Pilate.basis: Roman governors dealt with provincials in Greek; Latin was the language of the army and of his own inscription at Caesarea. The title on the cross was in Hebrew, Latin and Greek (19:20).

the disciples.basis: Galilean fishermen; Peter's Galilean speech was recognisable (Matthew 26:73). Andrew and Philip bear Greek names and came from Bethsaida, so were likely bilingual.

Andrew.basis: Galilean from Bethsaida; Greek name, likely bilingual; John has him say 'Messias' and glosses it.

Philip.basis: Galilean from Bethsaida; Greek name; the Greeks approach him (12:21), which suggests he spoke Greek too.

Nathanael.basis: From Cana in Galilee (21:2); addresses Jesus as 'Rabbi'.

Peter.basis: Renamed Kepha (Aramaic 'rock'), which John keeps as Kephas and translates (1:42).

the steward.basis: A village wedding at Cana in Galilee.

they.basis: Jewish interlocutors in Judea or Galilee (here: priests and Levites from Jerusalem, then two disciples of the Baptist).

the Jews.basis: Jerusalem authorities and crowds; Hebrew for scripture and legal debate is also possible.

the Pharisees.basis: Legal debate may have used Hebrew (Mishnaic Hebrew was a living language).

aramaic_words.ραββι: rabbi: 'my great one', teacher (John translates it at 1:38)
aramaic_words.αμην: amen: 'truly', a Hebrew/Aramaic word left untranslated; doubled only in John
